samples.summary: Dry-run's dot-segment backstop misses percent-encoded spellings (%2e/%2E), which the WHATWG URL parser resolves identically
samples.evidence: `assertNoDotSegments` compares each segment against the literal strings '.' and '..' only. Per the WHATWG URL spec a "double-dot path segment" is any of `..`, `.%2e`, `%2e.`, `%2e%2e` (ASCII case-insensitive) and a single-dot segment is `.` or `%2e`, all of which the parser resolves. `seg()` itself is safe because `encodeURIComponent` turns `%` into `%25` before any of those spellings can survive — but this function is documented as the backstop for a *future call site that forgets to call `seg()`* (see the header comment at dry-run.ts:15-18 and url.ts:9-14). For that exact case the backstop fails: a forgetful caller interpolating an argv-supplied doc id of `%2e%2e/%2e%2e/workspaces/other-ws/api-keys/key-1` passes the check and `printDryRun` prints a URL that, when copied into curl/an agent's fetch, normalizes out of the `/api/v1/workspaces/<ws>` base — precisely the outcome the guard exists to prevent. Not reachable through any shipped command today (every call site does encode), so this is a defense-in-depth gap in a guard advertised as complete, not a live exploit.

samples.summary: `--dry-run` prints the configured server URL unredacted, leaking `--server https://user:pw@host` credentials to stdout
samples.evidence: Line 29 (touched by this change) builds `${server}/api/v1/workspaces/...` straight from `config.server` and line 40 prints it with `console.log`. The CLI treats userinfo in `--server` as a secret everywhere else: `packages/cli/src/errors.ts:94-112` (`redactUrl`) exists specifically because "`user:pw@host` (what `--server user:pw@host` builds)" must never reach an error message, and every network error message routes through it. `--dry-run` output is the one thing agents are told to capture and log, so a credentialed `--server` (or a pre-signed query on it) lands in agent transcripts/CI logs in plaintext. Pre-existing on this line, but the change is what re-touched the URL construction; the fix is `redactUrl(server)` for the previewed URL. Note `status` (commands/status.ts:49) prints `session.server` the same way, so this is a pattern rather than a one-off.

samples.summary: `reportSkippedImage` writes document- and remote-server-controlled text to stderr with only C0/DEL stripping, unlike the JSON envelope path
samples.evidence: `oneLine` (line 709-715) strips `�-` and ``, then `reportSkippedImage` (line 727-730) emits the result with a bare `console.warn`, not `JSON.stringify`. Both interpolated fields are attacker-influenced: `src` is document content (an image `src` in a doc an agent or another user authored) and `reason` can carry a remote server's wording. The filter leaves C1 controls (U+0080–U+009F, notably U+009B CSI), U+2028/U+2029 line separators, and bidi overrides (U+202E) intact, so a crafted `src` can inject extra apparent lines into the same stderr stream an agent parses for the `{error:{code,...}}` envelope, or reorder the displayed text. Contrast the error path, where `JSON.stringify` escapes control characters (formatter.ts:315). Impact is limited to stderr spoofing/log confusion, not code execution. Note also that `oneLine` is applied to `redactUrl(src)`, so credentials in the src are correctly stripped first.

samples.summary: Opt-in image tolerance silently removes content from exports on any fetch OR decode failure, giving an attacker a lever to drop chosen content from a document a human treats as authoritative
samples.evidence: The new `try` at line 81 spans the fetch (82), the body read (83), the MIME sniff (89) and the pdf-lib embed calls (91-97); the `catch` at 99-102 reports and drops the image whenever `onImageError` was supplied. `DocxExporter.collectImages` (packages/docs/src/export/docx-exporter.ts:470-481) and `exportPptx` (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:172-187) do the same, and every CLI export path opts in (`docs/pdf-export.ts:116`, `docs/docx-export.ts:37`, `slides/pptx-export.ts:20`). The only signal is a `console.warn` line on stderr, which agents driving the CLI routinely discard while keeping stdout. So anyone who controls an image `src` in a shared document — or who can make one host unreachable — can cause named content to be omitted from a PDF/DOCX/PPTX that the recipient reads as complete. The lessons file added by this change (docs/tasks/active/20260811-cli-upstream-error-envelope-lessons.md) acknowledges the decode/embed over-scoping as a known caveat; it is recorded here as an integrity finding rather than a correctness nit because the dropped content is silent by design.

samples.summary: The only direct unit test of the new shared `seg()` security primitive lives in a package whose vitest suite no lane runs
samples.evidence: This change moves the security rule into `packages/core/src/url/index.ts` and adds `describe('seg')` (packages/core/test/url.test.ts:30-43) asserting the traversal encoding and the `.`/`..` refusal. The root `test` script (package.json:9) runs sheets, slides, frontend, backend, cli, docs and notes — core is absent — and no workflow under .github filters `@wafflebase/core`, matching the reviewer brief's note that core's suite exists but no lane invokes it. Only `tsc` (via core's build) touches the package. The rule therefore has no executing test at its canonical home; if someone widens or removes the refusal set there, the change is caught only incidentally by packages/frontend/src/api/url.test.ts and packages/cli/test/dry-run.test.ts. Since the whole point of hoisting `seg()` was that 'a rule enforced by two copies drifts', the shared copy should be the one with running tests.

samples.summary: Browser export fetches arbitrary document-controlled image URLs with `credentials: "include"` and no protocol/address gate — the counterpart the CLI's SSRF guard exists for
samples.evidence: `docsImageFetcher` resolves an image `src` taken verbatim from document content (`resolveImageUrl` at line 12-18 passes through any absolute URL, including `http://127.0.0.1:9200/...`, `http://169.254.169.254/...` or `https://attacker.example/`) and issues `fetch(resolved, { credentials: 'include' })` at line 51, embedding the bytes into the exported file. There is no `isSafeUrl`/address check on this path, while the CLI gates the same content through `assertFetchableImageUrl` + address pinning. A shared document can thus make a victim's browser probe and exfiltrate-by-embedding intranet/loopback resources it can reach, and send its cookies to a third-party origin. Pre-existing and outside the diff, but this change's own design docs now state the contract ('there no SSRF guard makes a refusal ordinary', docs/design/docs/docs-pdf-export.md), which makes the asymmetry a deliberate, documented gap worth a ticket. Confidence is low on exploit value: cookies sent are the *target* origin's, so no Wafflebase credential leaks, and cross-origin responses are CORS-blocked for anything that does not opt in.

finding.summary: Reviewer did not produce a valid verdict: review: every credential in the pool (2) was retired — nothing left to fail over to

verdict.reason: The finding text is not a claim about repository code - it is the review harness's own no-verdict record. I traced it to scripts/agent/ask.mjs:630-637 (poolExhaustedError, which produces the exact string "every credential in the pool (N) was retired - nothing left to fail over to") wrapped by scripts/agent/review-panel.mjs:1690-1695 with the "Reviewer did not produce a valid verdict: " prefix, taken because poolExhaustedError sets only kind/retryable and no `infra` flag (ask.mjs:634-635). There is no security vector to verify: no file, no attacker path, and the message contains only a label and pool size and passes through redactSecrets, so no secret leaks. I am still not refuting it, because refuting removes it from the merge gate and this repository deliberately fails closed on exactly this record: review-panel.mjs:1684-1688 states that a plain (non-infra) no-verdict "IS an ordinary fail-closed blocker", and scripts/agent/review-round-guard.mjs:186-190 pages a human ("A review lens did not produce a valid verdict. A human should review PR #<n>.") rather than letting the round pass. Since the Security lens never actually ran, dropping this would merge the change with zero security review - the outcome the fail-closed design exists to prevent. No named refutation ground applies (the code is present as described and reachable), so the finding stays.
